Rank functions, ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-extensions and class numbers

Iq Souza Address: University of Manchester, Manchester, United Kingdom Email address: henrique.souza@manchester.ac.uk
Date: October 27, 2026
Abstract.

If FF is a number field and F=F0⊂F1⊂F2⊂⋯F=F_{0}\subset F_{1}\subset F_{2}\subset\cdots is a tower of Galois extensions with Gal⁡(Fn/F)\mathrm{Gal}(F_{n}/F) cyclic of order pnp^{n}, K. Iwasawa gave a closed formula for the growth of the pp-part of the class number of FnF_{n} whenever nn is large enough. We present a new proof of this formula, obtained by reinterpreting its summands in terms of Sylvester matrix rank functions on the Iwasawa algebra Λ\Lambda without resorting to the classification of finitely-generated Λ\Lambda-modules up to pseudo-isomorphism.

1. Introduction

The purpose of this expository note is to show how some of the results in the Iwasawa theory of ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-extensions of number fields can be interpreted in the language of Sylvester rank functions.

In the mid 1950’s, Kenkichi Iwasawa was interested in the following question: given a tower F=F0⊂F1⊂F2⊂⋯F=F_{0}\subset F_{1}\subset F_{2}\subset\cdots of number fields, how does the size of the class group Cl⁡(Fi)\mathrm{Cl}(F_{i}) grow? Recall that the ideal class group Cl⁡(K)\mathrm{Cl}(K) of a number field KK with ring of integers 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} is defined as the quotient JK/PKJ_{K}/P_{K}, where JKJ_{K} is the group of fractional ideals of 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} and PKP_{K} is the subgroup of principal ideals. This is always a finite group, and it measures precisely the failure of unique factorization in 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K}.

In 1956, he gave a talk titled “A theorem on Abelian groups and its application in algebraic number theory.” on the Summer Meeting of the American Mathematical Society in Seattle. In his talk, he annouced the following remarkable theorem:

Theorem 1.1 ([2]).

Let FF be a number field, and F=F0⊂F1⊂F2⊂⋯F=F_{0}\subset F_{1}\subset F_{2}\subset\cdots be a tower of finite normal extensions of FF such that for L=⋃i≥0FiL=\bigcup_{i\geq 0}F_{i} we have Gal⁡(L/F)≃ℤp\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}. For each nn, let LnL_{n} be the subfield of LL fixed by pn​ℤpp^{n}\mathbb{Z}_{p} and penp^{e_{n}} be the highest power of pp dividing the order of the class group Cl⁡(Ln)\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n}). Then, there exist integers ν\nu, λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and μ≥0\mu\geq 0 such that

en=μ​pn+λ​n+νe_{n}=\mu p^{n}+\lambda n+\nu

for sufficiently large nn.

The main algebraic ingredient in a standard modern proof of Iwasawa’s theorem is a classification of finitely generated ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]-modules. Taking G=ℤpG=\mathbb{Z}_{p}, although the completed group ring ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!] is not a principal ideal domain, it behaves very similarly to one. For every finitely generated ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]-module MM, there are elements f1,…,fn∈ℤp​[[G]]f_{1}\,,\ldots\,,f_{n}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!] and a ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]-module homomorphism φ:M→(⨁ℤp​[[G]]/(fi))⊕ℤp​[[G]]m\varphi\colon M\to\left(\bigoplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]/(f_{i})\right)\oplus\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]^{m} such that ker⁡φ\ker\varphi and coker⁡φ\operatorname{coker}\varphi are both finite; this is the so called classification of ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]-modules up to pseudo-isomorphism. Thus, up to a finite constant error, it suffices to check Theorem 1.1 on modules of the form ℤp​[[G]]/(fi)\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]/(f_{i}). Such modules are very easy to describe since ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!] is a unique factorization domain.

Our goal is to give a proof of Theorem 1.1 without resorting to the classification of ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]-modules up to pseudo-isomorphism. The way to go about this is to study three natural families of rank functions on ring ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!] and to realize the quantities appearing in Theorem 1.1 as the “rescaled sides” of a triangle formed by points in these three families (to made clear in Section 3). These families all accumulate in a common, canonical rank function on ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!], and computing the precise rate of convergence for this accumulation yields Iwasawa’s formula.

The structure of this note is as follows: we collect in Section 2 the definition of Sylvester rank functions and some basic examples, the facts about the Iwawasa algebra ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!] that will be used as well as the input from Global Class Field Theory that allows us to deduce information about the ideal class groups along the tower L/FL/F. In Section 3, we define the three families of Sylvester rank functions on ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!] which capture the quantities in Theorem 1.1, and we prove this precise relation in Corollary 3.8. We then show how this Corollary immediately yields Theorem 1.1 for the case where FF contains a single prime over pp, totally ramified in LL, in Section 4. The adaptations requried to treat the general case are presented in Section 5.

2. Preliminaries

2.1. Sylvester rank functions

For this subection, we let RR denote an associative ring with unity, not necessarily commutative. We denote the space of all matrices of size n×mn\times m over RR by Matn×m​(R)\mathrm{Mat}_{n\times m}(R). For square matrices of size n×nn\times n, we use the shorthand Matn​(R)\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(R). The set Mat⁡(R)\mathrm{Mat}(R) denotes the set of all matrices over RR of any size, not necessarily square.

Definition 2.1.

A Sylvester matrix rank function is a map rk:Mat⁡(R)→ℝ≥0\operatorname{rk}\colon\mathrm{Mat}(R)\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} assigning to each matrix AA over RR a non-negative real number rk⁡(A)\operatorname{rk}(A) satisfying:

  1. (SMat1)

    rk⁡(0)=0\operatorname{rk}(0)=0 and rk⁡(1)=1\operatorname{rk}(1)=1;

  2. (SMat2)

    rk⁡(A​B)≤min⁡{rk⁡(A),rk⁡(B)}\operatorname{rk}(AB)\leq\min\{\operatorname{rk}(A)\,,\operatorname{rk}(B)\} for any pair of matrices A,B∈Mat⁡(R)A\,,B\in\mathrm{Mat}(R) which can be multiplied;

  3. (SMat3)

    rk⁡(A00B)=rk⁡(A)+rk⁡(B)\operatorname{rk}\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ 0&B\end{pmatrix}=\operatorname{rk}(A)+\operatorname{rk}(B) for any pair of matrices AA and BB;

  4. (SMat4)

    rk⁡(AC0B)≥rk⁡(A)+rk⁡(B)\operatorname{rk}\begin{pmatrix}A&C\\ 0&B\end{pmatrix}\geq\operatorname{rk}(A)+\operatorname{rk}(B) for any trio of matrices AA, BB and CC of the appropriate sizes.

If RR is a field and rk\operatorname{rk} is the usual notion of rank from linear algebra (i.e. number of pivots in a row-echelon form), then axioms (SMat1) through (SMat4) hold. In fact, in this case, rk\operatorname{rk} is the unique Sylvester matrix rank function defined on RR: it follows from (SMat2) that rk⁡(U)=n\operatorname{rk}(U)=n for any invertible matrix U∈Matn​(R)U\in\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(R), and again that rk⁡(U​A)=rk⁡(A​V)=rk⁡(A)\operatorname{rk}(UA)=\operatorname{rk}(AV)=\operatorname{rk}(A) for any matrix AA and any pair (U,V)(U,V) of invertible matrices of the appropriate sizes. Thus, for an arbitrary rank function rk\operatorname{rk}, rk⁡(A)\operatorname{rk}(A) is determined by the rank of any row-echelon form. This must in turn coincide with the number of pivots by (SMat1) and (SMat3).

Let ℳ\mathcal{M} denote the set of isomorphism classes of finitely presented right RR-modules. Rank functions can also be defined in ℳ\mathcal{M}:

Definition 2.2.

A Sylvester module rank function is a map dim:ℳ→ℝ≥0\dim\colon\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} assigning to each finitely presented right RR-module MM a non-negative real number dim(M)\dim(M) satisfying:

  1. (SMod1)

    dim(0)=0\dim(0)=0, dim(R)=1\dim(R)=1;

  2. (SMod2)

    dim(M⊕N)=dim(M)+dim(N)\dim(M\oplus N)=\dim(M)+\dim(N);

  3. (SMod3)

    For any exact sequence

    M′→M→M′′→0M^{\prime}\to M\to M^{\prime\prime}\to 0

    of finitely presented modules we have

    dim(M′′)≤dimM≤dimM′+dimM′′.\dim(M^{\prime\prime})\leq\dim M\leq\dim M^{\prime}+\dim M^{\prime\prime}\,.

Observe that if RR is Noetherian, then ℳ\mathcal{M} coincides with the class of all finitely generated right RR-modules. This will be the case for all rings considered in this paper. There is a natural connection between matrix rank functions and module rank functions:

Definition 2.3.

Let dim\dim be a Sylvester module rank function, and for any matrix A∈Matm×n​(R)A\in\mathrm{Mat}_{m\times n}(R) define the associated matrix rank function

rkdim⁡(A)=m−dim(Rm/A​Rn).\operatorname{rk}_{\dim}(A)=m-\dim(R^{m}/AR^{n})\,.

Conversely, if rk\operatorname{rk} is a Sylvester matrix rank function on RR and M≃Rm/A​RnM\simeq R^{m}/AR^{n} is a finitely-presented right RR-module, define the associated module rank function

dimrk(M)=m−rk⁡(A).\dim_{\operatorname{rk}}(M)=m-\operatorname{rk}(A)\,.
Proposition 2.4 ([6, Prop. 3.1.4]).

The associated module rank function dimrk(M)\dim_{\operatorname{rk}}(M) does not depend on the choice of presentation M≃Rm/A​RnM\simeq R^{m}/AR^{n}, and is a Sylvester module rank function on RR. The associated matrix rank function rkdim\operatorname{rk}_{\dim} is also a Sylvester matrix rank function, and the maps

dim↦rkdim,rk↦dimrk\dim\mapsto\operatorname{rk}_{\dim}\,,\quad\operatorname{rk}\mapsto\dim_{\operatorname{rk}}

induce bijections between the sets of Sylvester module rank functions and Sylvester matrix rank functions on any given ring RR.

We shall denote by ℙ⁡(R)\mathbb{P}(R) the set of all Sylvester matrix/module rank functions on a ring RR, where an associated pair rk/dim\operatorname{rk}/\dim represents the same element of ℙ⁡(R)\mathbb{P}(R). It is a convex, compact subspace of a real vector space. For any matrix AA over RR, the function

dA​(rk,rk′)=|rk⁡(A)−rk′⁡(A)|d_{A}(\operatorname{rk},\operatorname{rk}^{\prime})=|\operatorname{rk}(A)-\operatorname{rk}^{\prime}(A)|

defines a pseudo-metric on the set ℙ⁡(R)\mathbb{P}(R). We say that a sequence rki∈ℙ⁡(R)\operatorname{rk}_{i}\in\mathbb{P}(R) converges pointwise to a rank function rk∈ℙ⁡(R)\operatorname{rk}\in\mathbb{P}(R) if dA​(rki,rk)→0d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{i},\operatorname{rk})\to 0 as i→∞i\to\infty for any matrix AA over RR.

Example 2.5.

Suppose that RR is commutative and N≠0N\neq 0 is an RR-module of finite length ℓR​(N)\ell_{R}(N). For any finitely presented RR-module MM, we have that M⊗RNM\otimes_{R}N is again an RR-module of finite length, and the map

M↦dimN(M)=ℓR​(M⊗RN)ℓR​(N)M\mapsto\dim_{N}(M)=\frac{\ell_{R}(M\otimes_{R}N)}{\ell_{R}(N)}

is a Sylvester module rank function on RR. The associated Sylvester matrix rank function is defined by

rkN⁡(A)=ℓR​(A​Nn)ℓR​N\operatorname{rk}_{N}(A)=\frac{\ell_{R}(AN^{n})}{\ell_{R}N}

for any matrix A∈Matm×n​(R)A\in\mathrm{Mat}_{m\times n}(R). ∎

Example 2.6.

Let φ:R→S\varphi\colon R\to S be a ring map and rk\operatorname{rk} be a Sylvester matrix rank function on SS. Then, φ#​rk⁡(A)=rk⁡(φ⁡(A))\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{rk}(A)=\operatorname{rk}(\varphi(A)) is a Sylvester matrix rank function on RR. If dim\dim is the associated Sylvester module rank function on SS, then

φ#​dim(M)=dim(M⊗RS)\varphi^{\#}\dim(M)=\dim(M\otimes_{R}S)

is the module rank function associated to φ#​rk\varphi^{\#}\operatorname{rk}. In particular, if RR is a subring of SS, the restriction of any rank function on SS to Mat⁡(R)\mathrm{Mat}(R) is again a rank function on RR. ∎

Example 2.7.

Let 𝔽\mathbb{F} be a field, V≠0V\neq 0 be a finite-dimensional 𝔽\mathbb{F}-vector space and φ:R→End𝔽​(V)\varphi\colon R\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{F}}(V) a ring homomorphism. Then, for any matrix AA over RR, the map

rkV⁡(A)=rk𝔽⁡(φ⁡(A))dim𝔽V\operatorname{rk}_{V}(A)=\frac{\operatorname{rk}_{\mathbb{F}}(\varphi(A))}{\dim_{\mathbb{F}}V}

is a Sylvester matrix rank function on RR. It is the pullback of the unique Sylvester matrix rank function on End𝔽​(V)\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{F}}(V), the rank over 𝔽\mathbb{F} normalized by dim𝔽V\dim_{\mathbb{F}}V. ∎

Example 2.8 ([6, Exmp. 3.1.10]).

Assume now that RR is commutative domain and that SS is a multiplicative set of non-zero elements in RR. If rk\operatorname{rk} is a Sylvester matrix rank function on RR, then it extends to a Sylvester matrix rank function on S−1​RS^{-1}R if and only rk⁡(x)=1\operatorname{rk}(x)=1 for any x∈Sx\in S. Moreover, this extension is unique. ∎

A particular consequence of the phenomena in Example 2.8 is the following result:

Proposition 2.9 ([6, Cor. 5.2.5]).

Let RR be a commutative domain with field of fractions 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, and rki\operatorname{rk}_{i} a sequence of Sylvester matrix rank functions on RR. Then, we have limi→∞rki=rk𝒬\lim_{i\to\infty}\operatorname{rk}_{i}=\operatorname{rk}_{\mathcal{Q}} if and only if

limi→∞rki⁡(x)=1\lim_{i\to\infty}\operatorname{rk}_{i}(x)=1

for all non-zero x∈Rx\in R.

2.2. Iwasawa algebras

Let Λ=ℤp​[[ℤp]]\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![\mathbb{Z}_{p}]\!] be the completed group ring of the pro-pp group ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}. If we write ℤp=⟨γ⟩¯\mathbb{Z}_{p}=\overline{\langle\gamma\rangle} and T=γ−1∈ΛT=\gamma-1\in\Lambda, then we can identify Λ\Lambda with the ring ℤp​[[T]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![T]\!] of formal power series in TT over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}. In particular, it is a local Noetherian domain with maximal ideal (p,T)(p,T). Recall that a distinguished polynomial f​(T)∈ℤp​[T]f(T)\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[T] is a monic polynomial of the form

f⁡(T)=Ts+p​as−1​Ts−1+⋯+p​a1​T+p​a0f(T)=T^{s}+pa_{s-1}T^{s-1}+\cdots+pa_{1}T+pa_{0}

for some coefficients a0,…,as−1∈ℤpa_{0}\,,\ldots\,,a_{s-1}\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}. In particular, the constant polynomial f⁡(T)=1f(T)=1 is distinguished. The following result is known as an instance of the Weierstrass preparation theorem:

Theorem 2.10 ([7, Thm. 7.3]).

For any non-zero f∈Λf\in\Lambda, there exists a unique distinguished polynomial h∈ℤp​[T]h\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[T] and a unit u∈Λ×u\in\Lambda^{\times} such that

f=pa​u​h​ for some integer ​a≥0.f=p^{a}uh\text{ for some integer }a\geq 0\,.

We will also make use of the Weierstrass division theorem for the power series ring Λ\Lambda.

Proposition 2.11 ([7, Prop. 7.2]).

For any f∈Λ∖p​Λf\in\Lambda\smallsetminus p\Lambda, if f=u​hf=uh with u∈Λ×u\in\Lambda^{\times} and hh distinguished, then Λ/(f)\Lambda/(f) is a free ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module of rank deg⁡h\deg h and basis 1,T,…,Tdeg⁡h−11\,,T\,,\ldots\,,T^{\deg h-1}.

Since the quotient Λ/(p)≃𝔽p​[[T]]\Lambda/(p)\simeq\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!] is also a domain, the ideal (p)(p) is prime and therefore we can consider the localization

Λ(p)={fh:f,h∈Λ,h∉(p)}.\Lambda_{(p)}=\left\{\frac{f}{h}\colon f\,,h\in\Lambda\,,h\not\in(p)\right\}\,.

We shall use the following facts about Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} and its quotients:

Lemma 2.12.

The ring Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} is a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer pp and residue field 𝔽p​((T))\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!) of Laurent power series in TT over 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. If MM is a finitely generated torsion Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}-module, then pa​M=0p^{a}M=0 for some integer a≥0a\geq 0 and

ℓΛ(p)​(M)=∑i=0a−1dim𝔽p​((T))(pi​M/pi+1​M).\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M)=\sum_{i=0}^{a-1}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!)}(p^{i}M/p^{i+1}M)\,.

In particular, ℓΛ(p)​(Λ(p)/(pk))=k\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(\Lambda_{(p)}/(p^{k}))=k for any k≥0k\geq 0.

Proof.

For an element fh\dfrac{f}{h} in Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} we can uniquely write f=pa​f0f=p^{a}f_{0} with f0∈Λ∖p​Λf_{0}\in\Lambda\smallsetminus p\Lambda and a∈ℤ≥0a\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}. In particular, f0f_{0} is a unit in Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}, which proves that any element in Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} factors a power of pp times a unit. If II is any non-zero ideal of Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}, then choosing x=pa​u∈Ix=p^{a}u\in I with u∈Λ(p)×u\in\Lambda_{(p)}^{\times} and aa minimal shows that I=(pa)I=(p^{a}): for any y=pb​u′∈Iy=p^{b}u^{\prime}\in I, we have a≤ba\leq b and therefore y=pa⋅pb−a​u′∈(pa)y=p^{a}\cdot p^{b-a}u^{\prime}\in(p^{a}). This shows that Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} is a discrete valuation ring with uniformizer pp. The residue field of Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} can then be identified with the fraction field of Λ/(p)≃𝔽p​[[T]]\Lambda/(p)\simeq\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!].

If M=⟨m1,…,mk⟩M=\langle m_{1}\,,\ldots\,,m_{k}\rangle as a Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}-module, then since all the mim_{i} are torsion elements, there exists a high enough power pap^{a} of pp that annihilates them: pa​m1=⋯=pa​mk=0p^{a}m_{1}=\cdots=p^{a}m_{k}=0. This proves that pa​M=0p^{a}M=0. This gives a finite filtration

M≥p​M≥p2​M≥⋯≥pa−1​M≥pa​M=0M\geq pM\geq p^{2}M\geq\cdots\geq p^{a-1}M\geq p^{a}M=0

whose successive quotients are finite-dimensional 𝔽p​((T))\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!)-vector spaces. Since 𝔽p​((T))\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!) is the only simple Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}-module, the claim about length follows. ∎

For every integer n≥0n\geq 0, let

ωn=γpn−1=(1+T)pn−1∈Λ.\omega_{n}=\gamma^{p^{n}}-1=(1+T)^{p^{n}}-1\in\Lambda\,.

Observe that each ωn\omega_{n} is a distinguished polynomial in TT of degree pnp^{n}. We can identify the quotient Λ/(ωn)\Lambda/(\omega_{n}) with the group ring ℤp​[ℤp/pn​ℤp]≃ℤp​[Cpn]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\mathbb{Z}_{p}/p^{n}\mathbb{Z}_{p}]\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}[C_{p^{n}}] of the cyclic group of order pnp^{n} over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}.

Lemma 2.13.

For every pair n≥0,k≥1n\geq 0\,,k\geq 1 of integers, the ring

Λ/(pk,ωn)≃(ℤ/pk​ℤ)​[Cpn]\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n})\simeq(\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z})[C_{p^{n}}]

is a local Artinian ring and a free ℤ/pk​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z}-module of rank pnp^{n}. Seen either as an Λ\Lambda-module or as a ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module, its length is

ℓΛ​(Λ/(pk,ωn))=ℓℤp​(Λ/(pk,ωn))=k​pn.\ell_{\Lambda}(\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n}))=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n}))=kp^{n}\,.

For any finitely generated Λ/(pk,ωn)\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n})-module MM, we have

ℓΛ/(pk,ωn)​(M)=ℓΛ​(M)=ℓℤp​(M)=logp⁡|M|=∑i=0k−1dim𝔽p(pi​M/pi+1​M).\ell_{\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n})}(M)=\ell_{\Lambda}(M)=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M)=\log_{p}|M|=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(p^{i}M/p^{i+1}M)\,.
Proof.

The isomorphism Λ/(pk,ωn)≃(ℤ/pk​ℤ)​[Cpn]\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n})\simeq(\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z})[C_{p^{n}}] is clear from the definitions. Since this is a finite ring, it is necessarily Artinian, and it is also local, being a quotient of the local ring Λ\Lambda. Its description as a group ring shows that it is free of rank pnp^{n} as a ℤ/pk​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z}-module.

Since Λ→Λ/(pk,ωn)\Lambda\to\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n}) is surjective, the only simple Λ/(pk,ωn)\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n})-module is 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, which also the only simple ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module, we get equality of lengths

ℓΛ/(pk,ωn)​(M)=ℓΛ​(M)=ℓℤp​(M)\ell_{\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n})}(M)=\ell_{\Lambda}(M)=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M)

for any finitely generated Λ/(pk,ωn)\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n})-module MM. The filtration

M≥p​M≥p2​M≥⋯≥pk−1​M≥pk​M=0M\geq pM\geq p^{2}M\geq\cdots\geq p^{k-1}M\geq p^{k}M=0

whose successive quotients are finite-dimensional 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}-vector spaces proves that

ℓℤp​(M)=∑i=0k−1dim𝔽p(pi​M/pi+1​M)=logp⁡|M|.\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M)=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}}(p^{i}M/p^{i+1}M)=\log_{p}|M|\,.

The formula for the length of the ring Λ/(pk,ωn)\Lambda/(p^{k},\omega_{n}) now follows, since its order is (pk)pn(p^{k})^{p^{n}}. ∎

We will also use the following result, which is a particular case of a theorem of M. Harris ([1]):

Proposition 2.14 (cf. [6, Thm. 5.2.6]).

Let MM be a finitely generated Λ\Lambda-module, and for each n≥0n\geq 0, put

dimnM=dimℚp((M/ωn​M)⊗ℤpℚp)pn.\dim_{n}M=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}((M/\omega_{n}M)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p})}{p^{n}}\,.

Then, the dimn\dim_{n} are Sylvester module rank functions on Λ\Lambda, and limn→∞dimn=dimΛ\lim_{n\to\infty}\dim_{n}=\dim_{\Lambda} where dimΛ(M)=dim𝒬(M⊗Λ𝒬)\dim_{\Lambda}(M)=\dim_{\mathcal{Q}}(M\otimes_{\Lambda}\mathcal{Q}) and 𝒬\mathcal{Q} is the field of fractions of Λ\Lambda.

Proof.

For each n≥0n\geq 0, consider the finite-dimensional ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}-vector space Vn=ℚp​[G/Gpn]V_{n}=\mathbb{Q}_{p}[G/G^{p^{n}}] of dimension pnp^{n}. The left action of GG on the quotient group G/GpnG/G^{p^{n}} induces a ring homomorphism Λ→Endℚp​(Vn)\Lambda\to\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(V_{n}), and by definition the functions dimn\dim_{n} are the pullbacks of the normalized dimension in Endℚp​(Vn)\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(V_{n}) as in Example 2.7. In particular, they are Sylvester module rank functions, and we denote by rkn\operatorname{rk}_{n} the associated Sylvester matrix rank function.

To prove that limn→∞dimn=dimΛ\lim_{n\to\infty}\dim_{n}=\dim_{\Lambda}, it suffices to prove that rkn⁡(x)→1\operatorname{rk}_{n}(x)\to 1 as n→∞n\to\infty for any non-zero x∈Λx\in\Lambda by Proposition 2.9. Using Theorem 2.10, we can write x=pa​u​hx=p^{a}uh where a≥0a\geq 0, u∈Λ×u\in\Lambda^{\times} is a unit and h∈ℤp​[T]h\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[T] is a distinguished polynomial. In particular, rkn⁡(x)=rkn⁡(h)\operatorname{rk}_{n}(x)=\operatorname{rk}_{n}(h). Note that by Proposition 2.11, ℚp[G/Gpn]≃Λ/(ωn)⊗ℤpℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p}[G/G^{p^{n}}]\simeq\Lambda/(\omega_{n})\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p} has {1,T,…,Tpn−1}\{1\,,T\,,\ldots\,,T^{p^{n}-1}\} as a basis. If k=deg⁡hk=\deg h, then multiplication by hh is injective on the subspace spanned by {1,T,…,Tpn−1−k}\{1\,,T\,,\ldots\,,T^{p^{n}-1-k}\}, which gives us the bounds

1≥rkn⁡(h)≥pn−kpn.1\geq\operatorname{rk}_{n}(h)\geq\frac{p^{n}-k}{p^{n}}\,.

As nn goes to infinity, the right hand side converges to 11, proving the claim. Hence, as in Example 2.8, we have limn→∞dimn=dimΛ\lim_{n\to\infty}\dim_{n}=\dim_{\Lambda} as desired. ∎

2.3. Global Class Field Theory

Let KK be a number field, that is, a finite extension of ℚ\mathbb{Q}, and denote by 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} its ring of integers. A fractional ideal of KK is a subset I⊂KI\subset K of the form r−1​Jr^{-1}J, where JJ is an ideal of 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K}. It is invertible if there exists another fractional ideal J⊂KJ\subset K such that I​J=𝒪KIJ=\mathcal{O}_{K}. The set of all invertible fractional ideals forms an abelian group JKJ_{K} under multiplication, and it contains the subgroup PKP_{K} of all principal fractional ideals 𝒪K​x\mathcal{O}_{K}x for non-zero x∈Kx\in K. The quotient Cl⁡(K)=JK/PK\mathrm{Cl}(K)=J_{K}/P_{K} forms an abelian group called the ideal class group of KK. The ring 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K} is a principal ideal domain if and only if Cl⁡(K)=1\mathrm{Cl}(K)=1. The class number of KK is the order h⁡(K)=|Cl⁡(K)|h(K)=|\mathrm{Cl}(K)| of its ideal class group, and is a measure of how much does unique factorization fails in the ring 𝒪K\mathcal{O}_{K}.

Assume that L/KL/K is a Galois extension of number fields with Galois group G=Gal⁡(L/K)G=\mathrm{Gal}(L/K). Recall the existence of a multiplicative Galois norm map NL/K:L→KN_{L/K}\colon L\to K given by

NL/K​(x)=∏σ∈Gσ⁡(x).N_{L/K}(x)=\prod_{\sigma\in G}\sigma(x)\,.

This norm map induces a homomorphism NL/K:JL→JKN_{L/K}\colon J_{L}\to J_{K} between the groups of fractional ideals by declaring NL/K​(I)N_{L/K}(I) to be the fractional ideal of KK generated by the set {NL/K​(x):x∈I}\{N_{L/K}(x)\colon x\in I\} for every fractional ideal II of LL. This map sends principal fractional ideals to principal fractional ideals, and thus descends to a homomorphism NL/K:Cl⁡(L)→Cl⁡(K)N_{L/K}\colon\mathrm{Cl}(L)\to\mathrm{Cl}(K) of ideal class groups.

Now, let F=F0⊂F1⊂F2⊂⋯F=F_{0}\subset F_{1}\subset F_{2}\subset\cdots be a tower of finite Galois extensions of a number field FF such that for L=⋃i≥0FiL=\bigcup_{i\geq 0}F_{i} we have G=Gal⁡(L/F)≃ℤpG=\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}. For each nn, let LnL_{n} be the subfield of LL fixed by pn​ℤpp^{n}\mathbb{Z}_{p}. For an abelian group AA, denote by A⁡(p)A(p) its pp-primary part, that is, the set of all elements annihilated by some power of pp. With the norm maps defined above, the class groups Cl⁡(Ln)\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n}) fit into an inverse system of abelian groups, and we let

X=lim←⁡Cl​(Ln)​(p).X=\varprojlim\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)\,.

Since each LnL_{n} is a Galois extension of FF, the Galois group GG acts continuously and compatibly with the norm maps on each Cl⁡(Ln)\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n}) endowed with the discrete topology.

We summarize in the following theorem the main results about XX that will be used to prove Theorem 1.1.

Theorem 2.15.

Let γ\gamma be a topological generator of G≃ℤpG\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}, and set ωn=γpn−1∈ℤp​[[G]]\omega_{n}=\gamma^{p^{n}}-1\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]. For any pair of non-negative integers n≥mn\geq m, let ηn,m=ωnωm\eta_{n,m}=\dfrac{\omega_{n}}{\omega_{m}}.

  1. (1)

    ([3, Thm. I.6.3], [4, Lem. 2.23]) Each Cl⁡(Ln)\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n}) is a finite group, so XX is a pro-pp abelian group with a continuous GG action. In particular, XX is a ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]-module.

  2. (2)

    ([3, Prop. VI.6.9]) The Artin symbol map identifies Cl​(Ln)​(p)\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p) with the Galois group of the maximal unramified abelian pro-pp extension of LnL_{n} in which all real places split completely, and XX with the Galois group Gal⁡(H/L)\mathrm{Gal}(H/L) of the maximal unramified abelian pro-pp extension HH of LL in which all real places split completely.

  3. (3)

    ([7, Prop. 13.2 and Lem. 13.3]) In each extension L/LnL/L_{n}, only primes above pp ramify, and at least one prime ramifies. Moreover, for large enough nn all ramified primes in L/LnL/L_{n} are totally ramified.

  4. (4)

    For each prime vv in LnL_{n} above pp, let Iv≤GpnI_{v}\leq G^{p^{n}} be the inertia group of vv under the extension L/LnL/L_{n}. If Σn:⨁v|pIv→Gpn\Sigma_{n}\colon\bigoplus_{v\mid p}I_{v}\to G^{p^{n}} denotes the map induced by the inclusions Iv≤GpnI_{v}\leq G^{p^{n}}, then there is an exact sequence

    (1) ker⁡Σn→X/ωn​X→Cl⁡(Ln)​(p)→coker⁡Σn→0.\ker\Sigma_{n}\to X/\omega_{n}X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)\to\operatorname{coker}\Sigma_{n}\to 0\,.
  5. (5)

    There exists a positive integer mm such that for any n≥mn\geq m the maps X→Cl​(Ln)​(p)X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p) are surjective. Moreover, if Yn=ker⁡(X→Cl⁡(Ln)​(p))Y_{n}=\ker(X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)), we have Yn=ηn,m​YmY_{n}=\eta_{n,m}Y_{m}.

Proof.

We will only prove (4) and (5), since the first three are explicitly stated in the cited references. For the proof of (4), we essentially follow the ideas in [4, pp. 46–47]. Let HH be the maximal unramified abelian pro-pp extension of LL in which all real places split completely, for each n≥0n\geq 0 put En=Gal⁡(H/Ln)E_{n}=\mathrm{Gal}(H/L_{n}) and Gn=Gal⁡(L/Ln)=GpnG_{n}=\mathrm{Gal}(L/L_{n})=G^{p^{n}}. The short exact sequence

1→X≃Gal⁡(H/L)→Gal⁡(H/F)→G→11\to X\simeq\mathrm{Gal}(H/L)\to\mathrm{Gal}(H/F)\to G\to 1

coming from (2) also gives us the short exact sequence

1→X→En→Gn→11\to X\to E_{n}\to G_{n}\to 1

of profinite groups for each n≥0n\geq 0. This sequence splits, and upon passing to the abelianization, we have the short exact sequence

0→X/ωn​X→Enab→Gn→0.0\to X/\omega_{n}X\to E_{n}^{\text{ab}}\to G_{n}\to 0\,.

For a prime vv in LnL_{n} above pp, choose a prime ww in HH above vv and let uu be its restriction to LL. Let Iv~\widetilde{I_{v}} be the inertia group I⁡(w/v)≤EnI(w/v)\leq E_{n} and IvI_{v} the inertia group I⁡(u/v)≤GnI(u/v)\leq G_{n}. Observe that Iv~\widetilde{I_{v}} only depends on ww up to conjugation in EnE_{n}, and IvI_{v} is independent of ww by the fact that GnG_{n} is abelian. Restriction gives us a surjective Iv~→Iv\widetilde{I_{v}}\to I_{v} whose kernel is the inertia group I⁡(w/u)≤XI(w/u)\leq X by [3, Prop. II.9.5]. However, H/LH/L is totally unramified, so the inertia group I⁡(w/u)I(w/u) is trivial. In particular, we can lift Σn\Sigma_{n} to a map ιn:⨁v|pIv→Enab\iota_{n}\colon\bigoplus_{v\mid p}I_{v}\to E_{n}^{\text{ab}} along the isomorphisms Iv~→Iv\widetilde{I_{v}}\to I_{v}.

By the definition of the inertia subgroups, im⁡(ιn)\operatorname{im}(\iota_{n}) is the subgroup of EnabE_{n}^{\text{ab}} corresponding to maximal abelian subextension of H/LnH/L_{n} unramified at all primes above pp. By (3), this means that this extension is completely unramified, which by (2) yields a natural isomorphism

Enab/im⁡(ιn)≃Cl⁡(Ln)​(p).E_{n}^{\text{ab}}/\operatorname{im}(\iota_{n})\simeq\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)\,.

Applying the snake lemma to the commutative diagram

gives the long exact sequence

0→ker⁡ιn→ker⁡Σn→X/ωn​X→Cl⁡(Ln)​(p)→coker⁡(Σn)→0,0\to\ker\iota_{n}\to\ker\Sigma_{n}\to X/\omega_{n}X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)\to\operatorname{coker}(\Sigma_{n})\to 0\,,

from which (4) follows.

For (5), let mm be such that all ramified primes in L/LmL/L_{m} are totally ramified, which exists by (3). Now apply [7, Lem. 13.15] to the extension L/LmL/L_{m}. ∎

3. The Iwasawa rank triangle

In this section, we keep the notations of Sections 2.1 and 2.2. In particular, G=ℤp=⟨γ⟩¯G=\mathbb{Z}_{p}=\overline{\langle\gamma\rangle} denotes the infinite pro-cyclic pro-pp group and Λ=ℤp​[[G]]≃ℤp​[[T]]\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![T]\!] is its completed group algebra, where T=γ−1T=\gamma-1. We also denote by ωn\omega_{n} the element γpn−1∈Λ\gamma^{p^{n}}-1\in\Lambda. We are interested in three families of Sylvester matrix rank functions on the Iwasawa Λ\Lambda, which will form our “Iwasawa rank triangle”.

  1. (A)

    The rank rkΛ\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda} coming from the embedding of Λ\Lambda into its field of fractions 𝒬=Frac⁡(Λ)\mathcal{Q}=\operatorname{Frac}(\Lambda). On a Λ\Lambda-module MM, it is given by

    dimΛM=dim𝒬M⊗Λ𝒬.\dim_{\Lambda}M=\dim_{\mathcal{Q}}M\otimes_{\Lambda}\mathcal{Q}\,.
  2. (B)

    For any integer k≥1k\geq 1, the Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}-module Λ(p)/(pk)\Lambda_{(p)}/(p^{k}) has length kk by Lemma 2.12, and thus induces a rank function rk(p),k\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k} on Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} as in Example 2.5. We also denote by rk(p),k\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k} its restriction to Λ\Lambda. On a Λ\Lambda-module MM, it is given by

    dim(p),k(M)=ℓΛ(p)​(M(p)/pk​M(p))k.\dim_{(p),k}(M)=\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)}/p^{k}M_{(p)})}{k}\,.
  3. (C)

    For any pair of integers k≥1k\geq 1 and n≥0n\geq 0, the ring Λ/(ωn,pk)\Lambda/(\omega_{n},p^{k}) is local Artinian of length k​pnkp^{n} by Lemma 2.13, and thus we have a rank function rkn,k\operatorname{rk}_{n,k} on Λ/(ωn,pk)\Lambda/(\omega_{n},p^{k}) as in Example 2.5. We also denote by rkn,k\operatorname{rk}_{n,k} its pullback to Λ\Lambda under the projection Λ→Λ/(ωn,pk)\Lambda\to\Lambda/(\omega_{n},p^{k}), and on a Λ\Lambda-module MM it is given by

    dimn,k(M)=ℓΛ/(ωn,pk)​(M/(ωn​M+pk​M))k​pn=logp⁡|M/(ωn​M+pk​M)|k​pn.\dim_{n,k}(M)=\frac{\ell_{\Lambda/(\omega_{n},p^{k})}(M/(\omega_{n}M+p^{k}M))}{kp^{n}}=\frac{\log_{p}|M/(\omega_{n}M+p^{k}M)|}{kp^{n}}\,.

By Proposition 2.9, we have that a sequence rki\operatorname{rk}_{i} of rank functions in ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda) converges to rkΛ\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda} if, and only if, limi→∞rki⁡(x)=1\lim_{i\to\infty}\operatorname{rk}_{i}(x)=1 for any non-zero x∈Λx\in\Lambda. It is not hard to see that this is the case for the families rk(p),k\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k} and rkn,k\operatorname{rk}_{n,k} as n,k→∞n\,,k\to\infty.

Lemma 3.1.

As rank functions on Λ\Lambda, we have:

limk→∞rk(p),k=rkΛ,\lim_{k\to\infty}\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}=\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda}\,,
limn→∞rkn,k=rk(p),k,\lim_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}=\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}\,,
limk→∞(limn→∞rkn,k)=rkΛ.\lim_{k\to\infty}\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}\right)=\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda}\,.
Proof.

Note that the third limit follows from the first two. For the first limit, it suffices to show that for each non-zero x∈Λx\in\Lambda we have rk(p),k⁡(x)→1\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(x)\to 1 as k→∞k\to\infty. By Theorem 2.10, we can write x=pa​u​hx=p^{a}uh where a≥0a\geq 0 is an integer, u∈Λ×u\in\Lambda^{\times} is a unit and h∈ℤp​[T]h\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[T] is a distinguished polynomial. Observe that both uu and hh are units in the ring Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}, and therefore for k≥ak\geq a:

rk(p),k⁡(x)\displaystyle\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(x) =rk(p),k⁡(pa)\displaystyle=\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(p^{a})
=ℓΛ(p)​(pa​Λ(p)/pk​Λ(p))k\displaystyle=\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(p^{a}\Lambda_{(p)}/p^{k}\Lambda_{(p)})}{k}
=k−ak.\displaystyle=\frac{k-a}{k}\,.

This clearly converges to 11 as k→∞k\to\infty.

For the second limit, by the compactness of ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda) choose a convergent subnet {rki=rkni,k}i∈I\{\operatorname{rk}_{i}=\operatorname{rk}_{n_{i},k}\}_{i\in I} with kk fixed, and let rk=limi∈Irki\operatorname{rk}=\lim_{i\in I}\operatorname{rk}_{i}. Denote by dimi\dim_{i} and dim\dim the associated Sylvester module rank functions. As in Example 2.8, if we show that dim(Λ/(x))=0\dim(\Lambda/(x))=0 for any x∈Λ∖(p)x\in\Lambda\smallsetminus(p), then dim\dim extends to a rank function on Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}. By Theorem 2.10, any such xx can be written as x=u​hx=uh where u∈Λ×u\in\Lambda^{\times} is a unit and h∈ℤp​[T]h\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[T] is a distinguished polynomial, and moreover

dimi(Λ/(x))=dimi(Λ/(h))=ℓΛ/(ωni,pk)​(Λ/(ωni,pk,h))k​pni=logp⁡|Λ/(ωni,pk,h)|k​pni.\dim_{i}(\Lambda/(x))=\dim_{i}(\Lambda/(h))=\frac{\ell_{\Lambda/(\omega_{n_{i}},p^{k})}(\Lambda/(\omega_{n_{i}},p^{k},h))}{kp^{n_{i}}}=\frac{\log_{p}|\Lambda/(\omega_{n_{i}},p^{k},h)|}{kp^{n_{i}}}\,.

By Proposition 2.11, Λ/(h,pk)\Lambda/(h,p^{k}) is a free ℤ/pk​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z}-module of rank deg⁡h\deg h. Thus:

dimi(Λ/(x))\displaystyle\dim_{i}(\Lambda/(x)) =logp⁡|Λ/(ωni,pk,h)|k​pni\displaystyle=\frac{\log_{p}|\Lambda/(\omega_{n_{i}},p^{k},h)|}{kp^{n_{i}}}
≤k​deg⁡hk​pni=deg⁡hpni→0.\displaystyle\leq\frac{k\deg h}{kp^{n_{i}}}=\frac{\deg h}{p^{n_{i}}}\to 0\,.

Hence, dim\dim (and, equivalently, rk\operatorname{rk}) extends to Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}, which is a principal ideal domain. Since any matrix AA over Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} can be put into a Smith normal form

U​A​V=(pa100⋯000pa20⋯0000pa3⋯00⋱000⋯00000⋯00) with ​U,V​ invertible over ​Λ(p),UAV=\begin{pmatrix}p^{a_{1}}&0&0&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&p^{a_{2}}&0&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&0&p^{a_{3}}&\cdots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\cdots&0&0\end{pmatrix}\quad\text{ with }U\,,V\text{ invertible over }\Lambda_{(p)}\,,

it suffices to prove that limi∈Irki⁡(pa)=rk(p),k⁡(pa)=max⁡{0,k−a}k\lim_{i\in I}\operatorname{rk}_{i}(p^{a})=\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(p^{a})=\dfrac{\max\{0,k-a\}}{k}. This is immediate, since

rki⁡(pa)\displaystyle\operatorname{rk}_{i}(p^{a}) =1−logp⁡|Λ/(ωni,pk,pa)|k​pni\displaystyle=1-\frac{\log_{p}|\Lambda/(\omega_{n_{i}},p^{k},p^{a})|}{kp^{n_{i}}}
=1−logp⁡|Λ/(ωni,pmin⁡{k,a})|k​pni\displaystyle=1-\frac{\log_{p}|\Lambda/(\omega_{n_{i}},p^{\min\{k,a\}})|}{kp^{n_{i}}}
=1−min⁡{k,a}​pnik​pni\displaystyle=1-\frac{\min\{k,a\}p^{n_{i}}}{kp^{n_{i}}}
=max⁡{0,k−a}k\displaystyle=\frac{\max\{0,k-a\}}{k}

is constant as a function of i∈Ii\in I. Since the convergent subnet {rki}i∈I\{\operatorname{rk}_{i}\}_{i\in I} was arbitrary, we have that rkn,k→rk(p),k\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}\to\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k} as n→∞n\to\infty. ∎

Using Lemma 3.1, we represent in Figure 1 how our three families of Sylvester rank functions sit inside the space ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda). The shape of this figure is our so called Iwasawa rank triangle. Our strategy for proving Theorem 1.1 will be to use the pseudo-metrics

dA​(rk,rk′)=|rk⁡(A)−rk′⁡(A)|d_{A}(\operatorname{rk},\operatorname{rk}^{\prime})=|\operatorname{rk}(A)-\operatorname{rk}^{\prime}(A)|

of Section 2.1 on the space ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda) to measure all three “sides” of this triangle, where AA will be an appropriately chosen matrix over Λ\Lambda related to the class groups Cl⁡(Fi)\mathrm{Cl}(F_{i}).

A remarkable fact about the Iwasawa rank triangle in Figure 1 is that, when measuring its sides under the pseudo-metrics dAd_{A}, it always degenerates.

Theorem 3.2.

Let AA be any matrix over Λ\Lambda and dAd_{A} be the corresponding pseudo-metric on the space ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda). Then, for any pair n≥0n\geq 0 and k≥1k\geq 1 of integers we have

dA​(rkΛ,rkn,k)=dA​(rkΛ,rk(p),k)+dA​(rk(p),k,rkn,k).d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k})=d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda},\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k})+d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k})\,.
Proof.

It suffices to prove the inequalities

rkn,k⁡(A)≤rk(p),k⁡(A)≤rkΛ⁡(A)\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}(A)\leq\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(A)\leq\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda}(A)

for any matrix A∈Matr×s​(Λ)A\in\mathrm{Mat}_{r\times s}(\Lambda) and any pair n≥0,k≥1n\geq 0\,,k\geq 1 of integers. We will first prove that rkΛ\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda} is the universal rank function on ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda) ([6, Def. 3.2.1]), that is, rkΛ\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda} is the greatest element of ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda) under the pointwise partial order: rkΛ⁡(A)≥rk′⁡(A)\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda}(A)\geq\operatorname{rk}^{\prime}(A) for any matrix AA and any rank function rk′∈ℙ⁡(Λ)\operatorname{rk}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{P}(\Lambda) (see also [6, Exmp. 4.1.5]).

Let mA:Λs→Λrm_{A}\colon\Lambda^{s}\to\Lambda^{r} be the map given by left multiplication by AA, and also denote by mA𝒬:𝒬s→𝒬rm_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}}\colon\mathcal{Q}^{s}\to\mathcal{Q}^{r} its extension to 𝒬\mathcal{Q}-vector spaces. We see Λs\Lambda^{s} and Λr\Lambda^{r} as naturally embedded inside 𝒬s\mathcal{Q}^{s} and 𝒬r\mathcal{Q}^{r} respectively, such that the restriction of mA𝒬m_{A}^{\mathcal{Q}} to Λs\Lambda^{s} is mAm_{A}. Let L=mA​(𝒬s)∩ΛrL=m_{A}(\mathcal{Q}^{s})\cap\Lambda^{r} and t=rkΛ⁡(A)t=\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda}(A), so that dim𝒬mA​(𝒬s)=t\dim_{\mathcal{Q}}m_{A}(\mathcal{Q}^{s})=t. Since Λ\Lambda is Noetherian, LL is a finitely generated Λ\Lambda-submodule of Λr\Lambda^{r}, and L∩p​Λr=p​LL\cap p\Lambda^{r}=pL.

Hence, L/p​LL/pL is a Λ/(p)\Lambda/(p)-submodule of (Λ/(p))r(\Lambda/(p))^{r}. As Λ/(p)≃𝔽p​[[T]]\Lambda/(p)\simeq\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!] is a discrete valuation ring, L/p​LL/pL must be free as a Λ/(p)\Lambda/(p)-module, say of rank ll. If we choose lifts x1,…,xlx_{1}\,,\ldots\,,x_{l} in LL of a basis of L/p​LL/pL, by Nakayama’s lemma they generate the Λ\Lambda-module LL. Then, the lifts x1,…,xlx_{1}\,,\ldots\,,x_{l} are also linearly independent over 𝒬\mathcal{Q}: clearing out the denominators and the common powers of pp in any relation

a1​x1+⋯+al​xl=0a_{1}x_{1}+\cdots+a_{l}x_{l}=0

over 𝒬\mathcal{Q} descends to a linear relation between their images in L/p​LL/pL with non-zero coefficients, a contradiction. Hence, LL is a free Λ\Lambda-module, necessarily of rank t=lt=l. Since mA​(Λs)≤L≃Λt≤Λrm_{A}(\Lambda^{s})\leq L\simeq\Lambda^{t}\leq\Lambda^{r}, we get a factorization A=B​CA=BC where B∈Matr×t​(Λ)B\in\mathrm{Mat}_{r\times t}(\Lambda) and C∈Matt×s​(Λ)C\in\mathrm{Mat}_{t\times s}(\Lambda). If rk\operatorname{rk} is any Sylvester rank function on Λ\Lambda, by (SMat2) we have

rk⁡(A)=rk⁡(B​C)≤min⁡{rk⁡(B),rk⁡(C)}≤t=rkΛ⁡(A),\operatorname{rk}(A)=\operatorname{rk}(BC)\leq\min\{\operatorname{rk}(B),\operatorname{rk}(C)\}\leq t=\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda}(A)\,,

as desired.

For the other inequality, we consider the subring Λn=ℤp​[[Gpn]]=ℤp​[[ωn]]\Lambda_{n}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G^{p^{n}}]\!]=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![\omega_{n}]\!] of Λ\Lambda. Then, using the coset decomposition G=⋃g∈G/Gpng​GpnG=\bigcup_{g\in G/G^{p^{n}}}gG^{p^{n}}, we see that Λ\Lambda is a free Λn\Lambda_{n}-module of rank pnp^{n} under the natural embedding Λn→Λ\Lambda_{n}\to\Lambda, so we can see AA as a matrix of size pn​r×pn​sp^{n}r\times p^{n}s over Λn\Lambda_{n}. If we take M~=Λr/A​Λs\widetilde{M}=\Lambda^{r}/A\Lambda^{s} and M=M~/pk​M~=Λr/B​Λs′M=\widetilde{M}/p^{k}\widetilde{M}=\Lambda^{r}/B\Lambda^{s^{\prime}} for some matrix B∈Matr×s′​(Λ)B\in\mathrm{Mat}_{r\times s^{\prime}}(\Lambda) we have

rkn,k⁡(A)=r−ℓΛ​(M/ωn​M)k​pn,rk(p),k⁡(A)=r−ℓΛ(p)​(M(p))k.\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}(A)=r-\frac{\ell_{\Lambda}(M/\omega_{n}M)}{kp^{n}}\,,\quad\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(A)=r-\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)})}{k}\,.

Thus, the inequality rkn,k⁡(A)≤rk(p),k⁡(A)\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}(A)\leq\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(A) is equivalent to

(2) ℓΛ​(M/ωn​M)≥pn​ℓΛ(p)​(M(p)).\ell_{\Lambda}(M/\omega_{n}M)\geq p^{n}\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)})\,.

On one hand,

ℓΛ​(M/ωn​M)=logp⁡|M/ωn​M|=ℓΛn​(M/ωn​M)=ℓℤp​(M/ωn​M).\ell_{\Lambda}(M/\omega_{n}M)=\log_{p}|M/\omega_{n}M|=\ell_{\Lambda_{n}}(M/\omega_{n}M)=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M/\omega_{n}M)\,.

On the other hand, Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)} is a free (Λn)(p)(\Lambda_{n})_{(p)}-module of rank pnp^{n} and the corresponding residue field extension 𝔽p​((T))/𝔽p​((ωn))\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!)/\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(\omega_{n})\!) has degree pnp^{n}, so that

ℓ(Λn)(p)​(M(p))\displaystyle\ell_{(\Lambda_{n})_{(p)}}(M_{(p)}) =∑i=0k−1dim𝔽p​((ωn))(pi​M(p)/pi+1​M(p))\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(\omega_{n})\!)}(p^{i}M_{(p)}/p^{i+1}M_{(p)})
=∑i=0k−1pn​dim𝔽p​((T))(pi​M(p)/pi+1​M(p))\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}p^{n}\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!)}(p^{i}M_{(p)}/p^{i+1}M_{(p)})
=pn​ℓΛ(p)​(M(p)).\displaystyle=p^{n}\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)})\,.

Thus, by the isomorphism (Λn)(p)⊗ΛnΛ≃Λ(p)(\Lambda_{n})_{(p)}\otimes_{\Lambda_{n}}\Lambda\simeq\Lambda_{(p)}, the inequality (2) is equivalent to

(3) ℓΛn​(M/ωn​M)≥ℓ(Λn)(p)​(M(p)).\ell_{\Lambda_{n}}(M/\omega_{n}M)\geq\ell_{(\Lambda_{n})_{(p)}}(M_{(p)})\,.

For each square submatrix CC of BB (again, seen as a matrix over Λn\Lambda_{n} of size pn​r×pn​s′p^{n}r\times p^{n}s^{\prime}), its determinant (detC)​(ωn)(\det C)(\omega_{n}) is a power series over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} in the variable ωn\omega_{n}. Since both Λn/(ωn)≃ℤp\Lambda_{n}/(\omega_{n})\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p} and (Λn)(p)(\Lambda_{n})_{(p)} are discrete valuation rings with respective valuations vpv_{p} and v(p)v_{(p)}, by taking Smith normal forms we have the identities:

ℓℤp​(M/ωn​M)=min⁡{vp​((detC)​(0)):C​ is a maximal square submatrix of ​B},\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M/\omega_{n}M)=\min\{v_{p}((\det C)(0))\colon C\text{ is a maximal square submatrix of }B\}\,,
ℓ(Λn)(p)​(M(p))=min⁡{v(p)​((detC)​(ωn)):C​ is a maximal square submatrix of ​B}.\ell_{(\Lambda_{n})_{(p)}}(M_{(p)})=\min\{v_{(p)}((\det C)(\omega_{n}))\colon C\text{ is a maximal square submatrix of }B\}\,.

The inequality (3) now follows, since v(p)​((detC)​(ωn))=lv_{(p)}((\det C)(\omega_{n}))=l implies that plp^{l} divides all the coefficients of (detC)​(ωn)(\det C)(\omega_{n}), so in particular plp^{l} divides its constant coefficient (detC)​(0)(\det C)(0). ∎

For finitely generated torsion Λ\Lambda-modules MM, Theorem 3.2 already gives some information on the growth of coinvariant quotients:

Corollary 3.3.

Let M≃Λr/A​ΛsM\simeq\Lambda^{r}/A\Lambda^{s} be a finitely generated torsion Λ\Lambda-module. Then, for any integer n≥0n\geq 0 and μ=ℓΛ(p)​(M(p))\mu=\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)}) we have

logp⁡|M/(ωn​M+pk​M)|=μ​pn+k​pn​dA​(rk(p),k,rkn,k)\log_{p}|M/(\omega_{n}M+p^{k}M)|=\mu p^{n}+kp^{n}d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k})

whenever k≥1k\geq 1 is large enough.

Proof.

Note that if rk,rk′\operatorname{rk}\,,\operatorname{rk}^{\prime} are Sylvester matrix rank functions on ℙ⁡(Λ)\mathbb{P}(\Lambda) with associated Sylvester module rank functions dim,dim′\dim\,,\dim^{\prime}, then

dA​(rk,rk′)=|rk⁡(A)−rk′⁡(A)|=|dim(M)−dim′(M)|.d_{A}(\operatorname{rk},\operatorname{rk}^{\prime})=|\operatorname{rk}(A)-\operatorname{rk}^{\prime}(A)|=|\dim(M)-\dim^{\prime}(M)|\,.

Therefore, given that dimΛ(M)=0\dim_{\Lambda}(M)=0, we get:

dA​(rkΛ,rkn,k)=|dimΛ(M)−dimn,k(M)|=logp⁡|M/(ωn​M+pk​M)|k​pn.d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k})=|\dim_{\Lambda}(M)-\dim_{n,k}(M)|=\frac{\log_{p}|M/(\omega_{n}M+p^{k}M)|}{kp^{n}}\,.

Since MM is torsion, then so is its localization M(p)M_{(p)}. Over the discrete valuation ring Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}, this means that pk0​M(p)=0p^{k_{0}}M_{(p)}=0 for some k0≥0k_{0}\geq 0. Hence, for k≥k0k\geq k_{0} we have

dA​(rkΛ,rk(p),k)\displaystyle d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda},\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}) =|dimΛ(M)−dim(p),k(M)|\displaystyle=|\dim_{\Lambda}(M)-\dim_{(p),k}(M)|
=ℓΛ(p)​(M(p)/pk​M(p))k\displaystyle=\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)}/p^{k}M_{(p)})}{k}
=ℓΛ(p)​(M(p))k=μk.\displaystyle=\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)})}{k}=\frac{\mu}{k}\,.

The statement now follows from Theorem 3.2. ∎

It now only remains to estimate the quantity dA​(rk(p),k,rkn,k)d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}) in the statement of Corollary 3.3, which we will be able to do very explicitly if we assume that the module MM presented by AA has finite coinvariants. We start with a couple of lemmmas.

Lemma 3.4.

Let MM be a finitely generated Λ\Lambda-module, for each j≥0j\geq 0 let

M⁡[(T,p)j]={x∈M:(T,p)j​x=0}M[(T,p)^{j}]=\left\{x\in M\colon(T,p)^{j}x=0\right\}

be the Λ\Lambda-submodule of elements annihilated by the ideal (T,p)j(T,p)^{j}. Then, the submodule

F⁡(M)=⋃j≥1M⁡[(T,p)j]F(M)=\bigcup_{j\geq 1}M[(T,p)^{j}]

is finite and contains every finite submodule of MM. Moreover, there exists n0n_{0} such that for any n≥n0n\geq n_{0} we have ωn​F​(M)=0\omega_{n}F(M)=0.

Proof.

Since MM is Noetherian, the chain M⁡[(T,p)j]M[(T,p)^{j}] stabilizes. Hence, there exists j≥1j\geq 1 such that F⁡(M)=M⁡[(T,p)j]F(M)=M[(T,p)^{j}]. As this is a finitely generated module over the finite ring Λ/(T,p)j\Lambda/(T,p)^{j}, it is finite. Conversely, if N≤MN\leq M is a finite submodule, then its annihilator AnnΛ⁡(N)\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda}(N) is a finite index ideal of Λ\Lambda, and therefore contains (T,p)i(T,p)^{i} for some i≥0i\geq 0. The final assertion follows from the fact that ωn→0\omega_{n}\to 0 in the profinite topology of Λ\Lambda, which coincides with its (T,p)(T,p)-adic topology. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Let PP be a finitely generated Λ\Lambda-module annihilated by a power of pp, and denote by P⁡[ωn]P[\omega_{n}] the submodule of PP annihilated by ωn\omega_{n}. Then, for every n≥0n\geq 0, both P/ωn​PP/\omega_{n}P and P⁡[ωn]P[\omega_{n}] are finite and

ℓℤp​(P/ωn​P)−ℓℤp​(P⁡[ωn])=pn​ℓΛ(p)​(P(p)).\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(P/\omega_{n}P)-\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(P[\omega_{n}])=p^{n}\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(P_{(p)})\,.

Moreover, P⁡[ωn]=F⁡(P)P[\omega_{n}]=F(P) for sufficiently large nn.

Proof.

Let k≥1k\geq 1 be such that pk​P=0p^{k}P=0. Then, both P/ωn​PP/\omega_{n}P and P⁡[ωn]P[\omega_{n}] are finitely generated modules over the finite ring Λ/(ωn,pk)≃(ℤ/pk​ℤ)​[Cpn]\Lambda/(\omega_{n},p^{k})\simeq(\mathbb{Z}/p^{k}\mathbb{Z})[C_{p^{n}}], and therefore are also finite. Denoting by χn​(P)=ℓℤp​(P/ωn​P)−ℓℤp​(P⁡[ωn])\chi_{n}(P)=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(P/\omega_{n}P)-\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(P[\omega_{n}]), we see that χn​(P)\chi_{n}(P) is additive under short exact sequences: if

0→P1→P2→P3→00\to P_{1}\to P_{2}\to P_{3}\to 0

is a short exact sequence of finitely generated Λ\Lambda-modules annihilated by a power of pp, then applying the snake lemma to the commutative diagram

yields the exact sequence

0→P1​[ωn]→P2​[ωn]→P3​[ωn]→P1/ωn​P1→P2/ωn​P2→P3/ωn​P3→0.0\to P_{1}[\omega_{n}]\to P_{2}[\omega_{n}]\to P_{3}[\omega_{n}]\to P_{1}/\omega_{n}P_{1}\to P_{2}/\omega_{n}P_{2}\to P_{3}/\omega_{n}P_{3}\to 0\,.

The alternating sum of their lengths is zero, and thus χn​(P2)=χn​(P1)+χn​(P3)\chi_{n}(P_{2})=\chi_{n}(P_{1})+\chi_{n}(P_{3}).

For each ii, let Qi=pi​P/pi+1​PQ_{i}=p^{i}P/p^{i+1}P, so that χn​(P)=∑i=0k−1χn​(Qi)\chi_{n}(P)=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\chi_{n}(Q_{i}). Observe that each ωn\omega_{n} acts on QiQ_{i} as multiplication by TpnT^{p^{n}}. Each QiQ_{i} is a finitely generated 𝔽p​[[T]]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!]-module, and if we write si=dim𝔽p​((T))Qi⊗𝔽p​[[T]]𝔽p​((T))s_{i}=\dim_{\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!)}Q_{i}\otimes_{\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!]}\mathbb{F}_{p}(\!(T)\!) we have an embedding 𝔽p​[[T]]si→Qi\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!]^{s_{i}}\to Q_{i} with finite cokernel. Hence:

χn​(Qi)\displaystyle\chi_{n}(Q_{i}) =χn​(𝔽p​[[T]]si)+χn​(Qi/𝔽p​[[T]]si)\displaystyle=\chi_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!]^{s_{i}})+\chi_{n}(Q_{i}/\mathbb{F}_{p}[\![T]\!]^{s_{i}})
=pn​si,\displaystyle=p^{n}s_{i}\,,

where in the last equality we use that any endomorphism of a finite length module has kernel and cokernel with same lengths. Thus:

χn​(P)=∑i=0k−1χn​(Qi)=pn​∑i=0k−1si=pn​ℓΛ(p)​(P(p))\chi_{n}(P)=\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}\chi_{n}(Q_{i})=p^{n}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}s_{i}=p^{n}\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(P_{(p)})

by Lemma 2.12. The final claims follows from Lemma 3.4. ∎

Lemma 3.6 (cf. [5, Lem. 2.4.6], [4, Lem. 2.48]).

Let LL be a finitely generated Λ\Lambda-module that is a free ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module of finite rank, and assume that some power of TT annihilates L/p​LL/pL. Then, there exists an integer n0n_{0} such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0} we have ωn+1​L=p​ωn​L\omega_{n+1}L=p\omega_{n}L.

Proof.

Let F:L→LF\colon L\to L be the endomorphism induced by the action of 1+T1+T. Since the action of TT is nilpotent modulo pp, we know that Fpn0≡id(modp2)F^{p^{n_{0}}}\equiv\operatorname{id}\pmod{p^{2}} for some integer n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1. For any n≥n0n\geq n_{0}, let

Sn=id+Fpn+⋯+F(p−1)​pn∈Endℤp​(L).S_{n}=\operatorname{id}+F^{p^{n}}+\cdots+F^{(p-1)p^{n}}\in\mathrm{End}_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L)\,.

Then, Sn≡p​id(modp2)S_{n}\equiv p\operatorname{id}\pmod{p^{2}}, and so we can write Sn=p​UnS_{n}=pU_{n} with Un≡id(modp)U_{n}\equiv\operatorname{id}\pmod{p}. In particular, UnU_{n} is an automorphism of LL, and we have

(Fpn+1−id)=(Fpn−id)​Sn=p⁡(Fpn−id)​Un.(F^{p^{n+1}}-\operatorname{id})=(F^{p^{n}}-\operatorname{id})S_{n}=p(F^{p^{n}}-\operatorname{id})U_{n}\,.

Hence:

ωn+1​L\displaystyle\omega_{n+1}L =(Fpn+1−id)​L\displaystyle=(F^{p^{n+1}}-\operatorname{id})L
=p⁡(Fpn−id)​Un​L\displaystyle=p(F^{p^{n}}-\operatorname{id})U_{n}L
=p​ωn​L.∎\displaystyle=p\omega_{n}L\,.\qed

We are now ready to finish estimating the bottom length of the Iwasawa triangle.

Theorem 3.7.

Let M≃Λr/A​ΛsM\simeq\Lambda^{r}/A\Lambda^{s} be a finitely generated torsion Λ\Lambda-module whose coinvariants M/ωn​MM/\omega_{n}M are finite for all sufficiently large nn. Then, there exist integers λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, ν\nu and n0n_{0} such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0} and all sufficiently large kk (depending on nn) we have

dA​(rk(p),k,rkn,k)=λ​n+νk​pn.d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k})=\frac{\lambda n+\nu}{kp^{n}}\,.
Proof.

Observe that the hypothesis imply that M/ωn​MM/\omega_{n}M is finite for every n≥1n\geq 1. For each i≥0i\geq 0, let M⁡[pi]M[p^{i}] denote the Λ\Lambda-submodule of MM consisting of elements annihilated by pip^{i}, and set

P=⋃i≥1M⁡[pi],L=M/P.P=\bigcup_{i\geq 1}M[p^{i}]\,,\quad L=M/P\,.

Then, LL is torsion-free as a ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module. Moreover, it is also finitely generated over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}: it is also torsion and finitely generated as a Λ\Lambda-module, so its annihilator AnnΛ⁡(L)\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda}(L) is non-zero. Taking any non-zero f∈AnnΛ⁡(L)f\in\operatorname{Ann}_{\Lambda}(L) and writing f=pa​u​hf=p^{a}uh by Theorem 2.10 where a≥0a\geq 0, u∈Λ×u\in\Lambda^{\times} and h∈ℤp​[T]h\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[T] is a distinguished polynomial, we see that

f​L=0⟹h​L=0fL=0\implies hL=0

by torsion-freeness over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}. Hence, LL is a quotient of (Λ/(h))r(\Lambda/(h))^{r}, which is finitely generated over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} by Proposition 2.11. Observe as well that some power of TT acts trivially on L/p​LL/pL, as h≡Tdeg⁡h(modp)h\equiv T^{\deg h}\pmod{p}. Write L≃ℤpℤpλL\simeq_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{\lambda} for λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, and observe that the inclusion P→MP\to M induces an isomorphism P(p)≃M(p)P_{(p)}\simeq M_{(p)} of Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}-modules as hh is a unit in Λ(p)\Lambda_{(p)}.

Since L/ωn​LL/\omega_{n}L is finite and LL is a finitely generated free ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module, we see that ker⁡(L​→ωn⋅​L)=0\ker(L\overset{\omega_{n}\cdot}{\to}L)=0. Applying the snake lemma to the commutative diagram

then yields the exact sequence

0→P/ωn​P→M/ωn​M→L/ωn​L→0.0\to P/\omega_{n}P\to M/\omega_{n}M\to L/\omega_{n}L\to 0\,.

By the additivity of length under short exact sequences, we get

ℓℤp​(M/ωn​M)=ℓℤp​(P/ωn​P)+ℓℤp​(L/ωn​L).\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M/\omega_{n}M)=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(P/\omega_{n}P)+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n}L)\,.

Observe that PP is annihilated by some power pap^{a} of pp: since MM is Noetherian, the ascending chain M⁡[pi]M[p^{i}] of submodules stabilizes. By Lemma 3.5, there exists an n1n_{1} such that we have F⁡(P)=P⁡[ωn]F(P)=P[\omega_{n}] and

ℓℤp​(P/ωn​P)=pn​ℓΛ(p)​(P(p))+ℓℤp​(P⁡[ωn])\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(P/\omega_{n}P)=p^{n}\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(P_{(p)})+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(P[\omega_{n}])

for any n≥n1n\geq n_{1}.

Fix for now an integer n≥n1n\geq n_{1} and let k=k⁡(n)k=k(n) be an integer large enough so that pk​(M/ωn​M)=pk​P=0p^{k}(M/\omega_{n}M)=p^{k}P=0. We have:

dA​(rk(p),k,rkn,k)\displaystyle d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}) =|dim(p),k(M)−dimn,k(M)|\displaystyle=|\dim_{(p),k}(M)-\dim_{n,k}(M)|
=|ℓΛ(p)​(M(p)/pk​M(p))k−ℓℤp​(M/(ωn​M+pk​M))k​pn|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)}/p^{k}M_{(p)})}{k}-\frac{\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M/(\omega_{n}M+p^{k}M))}{kp^{n}}\right|
=|ℓΛ(p)​(P(p))k−ℓℤp​(M/ωn​M)k​pn|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(P_{(p)})}{k}-\frac{\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(M/\omega_{n}M)}{kp^{n}}\right|
=|ℓΛ(p)​(P(p))k−pn​ℓΛ(p)​(M(p))k​pn−ℓℤp​(F​(P))k​pn−ℓℤp​(L/ωn​L)k​pn|\displaystyle=\left|\frac{\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(P_{(p)})}{k}-\frac{p^{n}\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)})}{kp^{n}}-\frac{\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(F(P))}{kp^{n}}-\frac{\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n}L)}{kp^{n}}\right|
=ℓℤp​(F⁡(P))+ℓℤp​(L/ωn​L)k​pn\displaystyle=\frac{\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(F(P))+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n}L)}{kp^{n}}

As ℓℤp​(F​(P))\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(F(P)) is a constant, it suffices to prove that

ℓℤp​(L/ωn​L)=λ​n+C\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n}L)=\lambda n+C

for some constant CC and nn greater than some constant n0≥n1n_{0}\geq n_{1}. By Lemma 3.6, we can choose n0n_{0} such that for any n≥n0≥n1n\geq n_{0}\geq n_{1} we have ωn+1​L=p​ωn​L\omega_{n+1}L=p\omega_{n}L. Hence:

ℓℤp​(L/ωn​L)\displaystyle\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n}L) =ℓℤp​(ωn0​L/ωn​L)+ℓℤp​(L/ωn0​L)\displaystyle=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(\omega_{n_{0}}L/\omega_{n}L)+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n_{0}}L)
=(∑m=n0n−1ℓℤp​(ωm​L/ωm+1​L))+ℓℤp​(L/ωn0​L)\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{m=n_{0}}^{n-1}\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(\omega_{m}L/\omega_{m+1}L)\right)+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n_{0}}L)
=(∑m=n0n−1ℓℤp​(L/p​L))+ℓℤp​(L/ωn0​L)\displaystyle=\left(\sum_{m=n_{0}}^{n-1}\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/pL)\right)+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n_{0}}L)
=(n−n0)​λ+ℓℤp​(L/ωn0​L)\displaystyle=(n-n_{0})\lambda+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n_{0}}L)
=λ​n+C​ for ​C=ℓℤp​(L/ωn0​L)−λ​n0.\displaystyle=\lambda n+C\text{ for }C=\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(L/\omega_{n_{0}}L)-\lambda n_{0}\,.

One can then take ν=C+ℓℤp​(F⁡(P))\nu=C+\ell_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}(F(P)). ∎

Corollary 3.8.

Let MM be a finitely generated torsion Λ\Lambda-module whose coinvariants M/ωn​MM/\omega_{n}M are finite for all sufficiently large nn. Then, there exist integers μ≥0\mu\geq 0, λ≥0\lambda\geq 0, ν\nu and n0n_{0} such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0} we have

logp⁡|M/ωn​M|=μ​pn+λ​n+ν.\log_{p}|M/\omega_{n}M|=\mu p^{n}+\lambda n+\nu\,.
Proof.

Let λ\lambda, ν\nu and n0n_{0} be the integers from Theorem 3.7, AA be a matrix presenting MM and take μ=ℓΛ(p)​(M(p))\mu=\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(M_{(p)}). By Corollary 3.3, for each n≥n0n\geq n_{0} and sufficiently large kk depending on nn we have:

logp⁡|M/ωn​M|\displaystyle\log_{p}|M/\omega_{n}M| =μ​pn+k​pn⋅dA​(rk(p),k,rkn,k)\displaystyle=\mu p^{n}+kp^{n}\cdot d_{A}(\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k},\operatorname{rk}_{n,k})
=μ​pn+k​pn⋅λ​n+νk​pn\displaystyle=\mu p^{n}+kp^{n}\cdot\frac{\lambda n+\nu}{kp^{n}}
=μ​pn+λ​n+ν.∎\displaystyle=\mu p^{n}+\lambda n+\nu\,.\qed

4. Totally ramified, single prime ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-extensions

We can now turn to the proof of Theorem 1.1. As such, we recall its notation: FF is a number field, F=F0⊂F1⊂F2⊂⋯F=F_{0}\subset F_{1}\subset F_{2}\subset\cdots is a tower of finite normal extensions of FF such that for L=⋃i≥0FiL=\bigcup_{i\geq 0}F_{i} we have G=Gal⁡(L/F)=⟨γ⟩¯≃ℤpG=\mathrm{Gal}(L/F)=\overline{\langle\gamma\rangle}\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}. For each n≥0n\geq 0, LnL_{n} denotes the subfield fixed by Gpn≃pn​ℤpG^{p^{n}}\simeq p^{n}\mathbb{Z}_{p} and penp^{e_{n}} is the highest power of pp dividing the order of the class group Cl⁡(Ln)\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n}). We let T=γ−1∈ℤp​[[G]]T=\gamma-1\in\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!], Λ=ℤp​[[G]]=ℤp​[[T]]\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![T]\!], ωn=γpn−1\omega_{n}=\gamma^{p^{n}}-1 and for any abelian group MM we denote by M⁡(p)M(p) its pp-primary part.

Bearing in mind the statement of Corollary 3.8, the ideal scenario would be to find a torsion ℤp​[[G]]\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G]\!]-module MM for which we have |M/ωn​M|=|Cl⁡(Ln)​(p)||M/\omega_{n}M|=|\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)| whenever nn is large enough. Unfortunately, there is no natural candidate for this MM in general (see (4) of Theorem 2.15). There is, however, a situation in which this module does exists: whenever there exists a single prime vv on LL over pp, and this prime is totally ramified.

It seems to be a tradition to first prove his formula in the totally ramified case, and then to follow through with general ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-extensions (see [4, Sec. 3.1.2]). This pedagogical choice also dates back to Iwasawa’s paper [2], which discusses a simplification of the proof under this particular hypothesis at the end. It is not the case that general extensions reduce to the totally ramified case, much to the contrary: the totally ramified case illustrates very clearly the mechanism behind Iwasawa’s formula, and the presence of other primes and residue-field extensions only introduce technicalities one has to work around. As such, we keep on with this tradition. Hence, consider the following hypothesis:

(HYP)

FF has a unique prime above pp, which is totally ramified in L/FL/F.

Proof of Theorem 1.1 assuming (HYP).

Let vv be the unique prime of LL over pp. In particular, for each n≥0n\geq 0, its restriction unu_{n} to LnL_{n} is the unique prime of LnL_{n} over pp as well. The assumption that L/FL/F is totally ramified at pp means that for each nn the inertia groups Iv,n=I⁡(v/un)I_{v,n}=I(v/u_{n}) of vv over LnL_{n} equals the whole Galois group GpnG^{p^{n}}, and the map Σn:Iv,n→Gpn\Sigma_{n}\colon I_{v,n}\to G^{p^{n}} of Theorem 2.15 is the identity. Hence, if X=lim←⁡Cl​(Ln)​(p)X=\varprojlim\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p) denotes the inverse limit of the pp-primary part of the class groups along the norm maps, by part (4) of Theorem 2.15 we have an isomorphism X/ωn​X≃Cl⁡(Ln)​(p)X/\omega_{n}X\simeq\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p) for each n≥0n\geq 0.

By Nakayama’s lemma ([6, Prop. 1.2.5]), a profinite Λ\Lambda-module MM is finitely generated if and only if M/(T,p)​MM/(T,p)M is finite. Since T=ω0T=\omega_{0}, we see that X/(ω0,p)​X≃Cl⁡(F)​(p)/p​Cl​(F)​(p)X/(\omega_{0},p)X\simeq\mathrm{Cl}(F)(p)/p\mathrm{Cl}(F)(p) is finite by part (1) of Theorem 2.15 and thus XX is finitely generated. By Proposition 2.14, we have

dimΛX=limn→∞dimℚp(X/ωn​X)⊗ℤpℚppn=0,\dim_{\Lambda}X=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\dim_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(X/\omega_{n}X)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p}}{p^{n}}=0\,,

so XX is torsion. By Corollary 3.8, there are integers μ≥0\mu\geq 0, λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 and ν\nu such that for large enough nn we have

en=logp⁡|X/ωn​X|=μ​pn+λ​n+ν.∎e_{n}=\log_{p}|X/\omega_{n}X|=\mu p^{n}+\lambda n+\nu\,.\qed

As established in the proof of Corollary 3.3 and Theorem 3.7, in this case we can express the constants μ\mu and λ\lambda in terms of the following “rank-theoretical” invariants of XX:

μ=ℓΛ(p)​(X(p)),λ=dimℚp(X⊗ℤpℚp).\mu=\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(X_{(p)})\,,\quad\lambda=\dim_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(X\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p})\,.

5. General ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-extensions

Keeping with the notation of Section 4, we now drop the hypothesis on how pp splits in FF or ramifies in LL. By parts (3) and (5) of Theorem 2.15, there exists an integer m≥0m\geq 0 such that all ramified primes in L/LmL/L_{m} are totally ramified and the maps X→Cl​(Ln)​(p)X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p) are surjective. Let 𝔭1,…,𝔭s\mathfrak{p}_{1}\,,\ldots\,,\mathfrak{p}_{s} be the primes in LmL_{m} which ramify in L/LmL/L_{m}. Thus, for any n≥mn\geq m, any prime vv of LnL_{n} that ramifies in L/LnL/L_{n} lies above a unique 𝔭i\mathfrak{p}_{i}, and there is only one prime of LnL_{n} above each 𝔭i\mathfrak{p}_{i}. We can therefore label the ramified primes of L/LnL/L_{n} by vn,1,…,vn,sv_{n,1}\,,\ldots\,,v_{n,s}, and in particular their quantity is bounded independently of nn.

For each vn,rv_{n,r}, its inertia subgroup Ivn,rI_{v_{n,r}} equals the whole Galois group GpnG^{p^{n}}, and thus Σn:⨁r=1sIvn,r→Gpn\Sigma_{n}\colon\bigoplus_{r=1}^{s}I_{v_{n,r}}\to G^{p^{n}} is simply the addition map ℤps→ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{s}\to\mathbb{Z}_{p}. In particular, ker⁡Σn≃ℤps−1\ker\Sigma_{n}\simeq\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{s-1} and coker⁡Σn=0\operatorname{coker}\Sigma_{n}=0. By part (4) of Theorem 2.15, we get the exact sequence

(4) ℤps−1→X/ωn​X→Cl⁡(Ln)​(p)→0.\mathbb{Z}_{p}^{s-1}\to X/\omega_{n}X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)\to 0\,.

Let Yn=ker⁡(X→Cl⁡(Ln)​(p))Y_{n}=\ker(X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)) and Y=YmY=Y_{m}. Recall from part (5) of Theorem 2.15 that for ηn,m=ωnωm\eta_{n,m}=\dfrac{\omega_{n}}{\omega_{m}} we have Yn=ηn,m​YY_{n}=\eta_{n,m}Y. In particular, for any n≥mn\geq m, we get two more short exact sequences

(5) 0→ηn,m​Y→X→Cl⁡(Ln)​(p)→00\to\eta_{n,m}Y\to X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)\to 0\,
(6) 0→Y/ηn,m​Y→Cl⁡(Ln)​(p)→Cl⁡(Lm)​(p)→0.0\to Y/\eta_{n,m}Y\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{n})(p)\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{m})(p)\to 0\,.

The short exact sequence (6) implies that Y/ηn,m​YY/\eta_{n,m}Y is finite, while the exact sequence (4) implies that Y/ωn​XY/\omega_{n}X is finitely generated as a ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module.

Lemma 5.1.

The Λ\Lambda-module XX is finitely generated and torsion.

Proof.

For each n≥mn\geq m, let Λn=ℤp​[[Gpn]]\Lambda_{n}=\mathbb{Z}_{p}[\![G^{p^{n}}]\!]. It suffices to prove that XX is finitely generated as a Λm\Lambda_{m}-module. Since it is profinite, by Nakayama’s lemma ([6, Prop. 1.2.5]) we once again see that it is finitely generated if and only if X/(ωm,p)​XX/(\omega_{m},p)X is finite. Tensoring the exact sequence (4) with 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p} over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} yields the exact sequence

𝔽ps−1→X/(ωm,p)​X→Cl⁡(Lm)/p​Cl​(Lm)→0.\mathbb{F}_{p}^{s-1}\to X/(\omega_{m},p)X\to\mathrm{Cl}(L_{m})/p\mathrm{Cl}(L_{m})\to 0\,.

Hence, X/(ωm,p)​XX/(\omega_{m},p)X is finite, and so XX is finitely generated.

Now, tensoring the exact sequence (4) with ℚp\mathbb{Q}_{p} over ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p} yields the exact sequence

ℚps−1→(X/ωn​X)⊗ℤpℚp→0,\mathbb{Q}_{p}^{s-1}\to(X/\omega_{n}X)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p}\to 0\,,

and so Proposition 2.14 gives us

dimΛ(X)=limn→∞dimℚp((X/ωn​X)⊗ℤpℚp)pn≤limn→∞s−1pn=0.\dim_{\Lambda}(X)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\dim_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}((X/\omega_{n}X)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p})}{p^{n}}\leq\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{s-1}{p^{n}}=0\,.

This proves that XX is torsion. ∎

In particular, all the Λ\Lambda-submodules YnY_{n} of XX are also finitely generated and torsion. We are now ready to prove the main theorem of this note. We will accomplish this by repeating the proof of Lemma 3.5, Lemma 3.6 and Theorem 3.7 with ηn,m\eta_{n,m} playing the role of ωn\omega_{n}, with the due changes noted.

Proof of Theorem 1.1.

Write

P=⋃i≥0Y⁡[pi],N=Y/P.P=\bigcup_{i\geq 0}Y[p^{i}]\,,\quad N=Y/P\,.

Since YY is Noetherian, the chain Y⁡[pi]Y[p^{i}] stabilizes, and thus there exists some a≥0a\geq 0 such that pa​P=0p^{a}P=0. As in the proof of Theorem 3.7, NN is finitely generated and free as a ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module, say of rank λ\lambda.

Since Y/ηn,m​YY/\eta_{n,m}Y is finite by the short exact sequence (6), we see that ker⁡(N​→ηn,m⋅​N)=0\ker(N\overset{\eta_{n,m}\cdot}{\to}N)=0. Applying the snake lemma to the commutative diagram

yields the short exact sequence

0→P/ηn,m​P→Y/ηn,m​Y→N/ηn,m​N→0.0\to P/\eta_{n,m}P\to Y/\eta_{n,m}Y\to N/\eta_{n,m}N\to 0\,.

Hence:

(7) en−em=logp⁡|Y/ηn,m​Y|=logp⁡|P/ηn,m​P|+logp⁡|N/ηn,m​N|.e_{n}-e_{m}=\log_{p}|Y/\eta_{n,m}Y|=\log_{p}|P/\eta_{n,m}P|+\log_{p}|N/\eta_{n,m}N|\,.

The proof of Lemma 3.5 applies verbatim with ηn,m\eta_{n,m} in place of ωn\omega_{n}, and since ηn,m≡Tpn−pm(modp)\eta_{n,m}\equiv T^{p^{n}-p^{m}}\pmod{p} it yields a constant n1≥mn_{1}\geq m for which whenever n≥n1n\geq n_{1} we have P⁡[ηn,m]=F⁡(P)P[\eta_{n,m}]=F(P) and

(8) logp⁡|P/ηn,m​P|=ℓΛ(p)​(P(p))​(pn−pm)+logp⁡|F⁡(P)|.\log_{p}|P/\eta_{n,m}P|=\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(P_{(p)})(p^{n}-p^{m})+\log_{p}|F(P)|\,.

We now finish as in Theorem 3.7 and Lemma 3.6. For n≥n0≥n1n\geq n_{0}\geq n_{1} where n0n_{0} is some constant, the element

ηn+1,n=1+γpn+⋯+γ(p−1)​pn\eta_{n+1,n}=1+\gamma^{p^{n}}+\cdots+\gamma^{(p-1)p^{n}}

acts on NN as an endomorphism Sn+1S_{n+1} satisfying Sn+1≡p​id(modp2)S_{n+1}\equiv p\operatorname{id}\pmod{p^{2}}, and so we can write Sn+1=p​Un+1S_{n+1}=pU_{n+1} with Un+1≡id(modp)U_{n+1}\equiv\operatorname{id}\pmod{p}. In particular, Un+1U_{n+1} is an automorphism of NN and we have that ηn+1,m=ηn+1,n​ηn,m\eta_{n+1,m}=\eta_{n+1,n}\eta_{n,m} satisfies ηn+1,m​N=p​ηn,m​N\eta_{n+1,m}N=p\eta_{n,m}N. These give

(9) logp⁡|N/ηn,m​N|=logp⁡|ηn0,m​N/ηn,m​N|+logp⁡|N/ηn0,m​N|=(∑k=n0n−1logp⁡|ηk,m​N/ηk+1,m​N|)+logp⁡|N/ηn0,m​N|=(∑k=n0n−1logp⁡|N/p​N|)+logp⁡|N/ηn0,m​N|=(n−n0)​λ+logp⁡|N/ηn0,m​N|.\begin{split}\log_{p}|N/\eta_{n,m}N|&=\log_{p}|\eta_{n_{0},m}N/\eta_{n,m}N|+\log_{p}|N/\eta_{n_{0},m}N|\\ &=\left(\sum_{k=n_{0}}^{n-1}\log_{p}|\eta_{k,m}N/\eta_{k+1,m}N|\right)+\log_{p}|N/\eta_{n_{0},m}N|\\ &=\left(\sum_{k=n_{0}}^{n-1}\log_{p}|N/pN|\right)+\log_{p}|N/\eta_{n_{0},m}N|\\ &=(n-n_{0})\lambda+\log_{p}|N/\eta_{n_{0},m}N|\,.\end{split}

We take

μ=ℓΛ(p)​(P(p)),λ=dimℚp(N⊗ℤpℚp)\mu=\ell_{\Lambda_{(p)}}(P_{(p)})\,,\quad\lambda=\dim_{\mathbb{Q}_{p}}(N\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_{p}}\mathbb{Q}_{p})
and ​ν=logp⁡|F⁡(P)|+logp⁡|N/ηn0,m​N|−n0​λ+em−μ​pm.\text{and }\nu=\log_{p}|F(P)|+\log_{p}|N/\eta_{n_{0},m}N|-n_{0}\lambda+e_{m}-\mu p^{m}\,.

Remark 5.2 (cf. [4, Rmk. 2.51]).

One could give uniform proof of Theorem 1.1 analogous to the totally ramified, single prime case if one first proves the results of Section 3 in a more general setting, at the expense of working with less explicit rank functions. Concretely, fix an integer m≥0m\geq 0 and a distinguished polynomial gg dividing ωm\omega_{m}, and for n≥mn\geq m put fn=ωngf_{n}=\dfrac{\omega_{n}}{g}. This includes both the families fn=ωnf_{n}=\omega_{n} with g=1g=1 and fn=ηn,mf_{n}=\eta_{n,m} with g=ωmg=\omega_{m}. One then replaces the rank functions rkn,k\operatorname{rk}_{n,k} by those induced from the finite length module Λ/(fn,pk)\Lambda/(f_{n},p^{k}). The following results are then shown by very similar arguments:

  • •

    (Lemma 3.1) For kk fixed, limn→∞rkn,k=rk(p),k\lim_{n\to\infty}\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}=\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}.

  • •

    (Theorem 3.2) rkn,k⁡(A)≤rk(p),k⁡(A)≤rkΛ⁡(A)\operatorname{rk}_{n,k}(A)\leq\operatorname{rk}_{(p),k}(A)\leq\operatorname{rk}_{\Lambda}(A) for any matrix AA over Λ\Lambda.

  • •

    (Lemma 3.6) Let LL be a finitely generated Λ\Lambda-module that is a free ℤp\mathbb{Z}_{p}-module of finite rank, and assume that some power of TT annihilates L/p​LL/pL. Then, there exists an integer n0n_{0} such that for all n≥n0n\geq n_{0} we have fn+1​L=p​fn​Lf_{n+1}L=pf_{n}L.

This allows one to establish a version of Corollary 3.8 for the growth of the modules M/fn​MM/f_{n}M of the form

logp⁡|M/fn​M|=μ​pn+λ​n+ν\log_{p}|M/f_{n}M|=\mu p^{n}+\lambda n+\nu

for large enough nn. Applying this to g=1g=1 and M=XM=X recovers Theorem 1.1 under the hypothesis (HYP) of Section 4, while applying it to g=ωmg=\omega_{m} and M=YM=Y recovers the argument in this section.
